Chapter 3: Understanding and Expressing Feelings—The Emotional Core of Difficult Conversations
Underneath every tough conversation, there’s almost always a swirl of emotions. Think about it—anger, sadness, fear, frustration... These feelings shape how we see things, the words we pick, and how we react, even if we don’t always realize it. But here’s the thing: in so many environments, especially at work, emotions kind of get pushed to the side. They’re treated like distractions, or even as something to hide. The truth? Emotions aren’t just background noise—they’re right at the heart of why conversations get tricky. When we don’t talk about what we’re feeling, those emotions still find ways to sneak out. Maybe it’s in our tone, a stiff posture, or a passive-aggressive comment. And if you keep pushing those feelings down, they tend to pile up. Before you know it, you’re carrying resentment, or suddenly you snap, and the whole conversation goes off the rails.
So, how do you deal with the emotional layer? It starts with a little self-awareness. First, try to recognize and actually name what you’re feeling—not just the obvious stuff, but also what might be bubbling underneath. For instance, sometimes anger is really just disappointment, hurt, or maybe even a fear of being rejected. Taking a moment to reflect before you speak can keep those emotions from spilling out in ways you didn’t intend.
Now, let’s talk about expressing those feelings. A lot of people worry that if they’re honest about their emotions, they’ll look weak, irrational, or too sensitive. But the opposite is usually true. When you share your feelings openly—without blaming—it can actually build trust and make others feel safe to open up too. The trick is to talk about what you feel as your own experience, not as an accusation.
Here are some practical tips for bringing feelings into the conversation:
Acknowledge that emotions are real and valid. They’re a natural response to things that matter, not a sign that you’ve failed or lost control. Describe your feelings instead of blaming. So instead of saying, “You make me angry,” try, “I feel frustrated when deadlines are missed, because I worry about the team’s progress.” Listen for what the other person might be feeling too. Notice if they seem hurt, anxious, or defensive. And invite them to share their side, so you’re not the only one putting your emotions on the table.
Imagine this: a friend cancels on you at the last minute. Maybe you’re irritated, or just plain disappointed. But if you dig a little deeper, you might realize you’re actually feeling overlooked or not that important to them. By saying something like, “I felt let down when our plans changed, because I was looking forward to seeing you,” you open the door for a real conversation and maybe even a stronger connection, instead of just conflict.
And don’t forget—it’s just as important to tune in to the other person’s feelings. Sometimes we get so wrapped up in our own emotions, we miss theirs completely. Ask open questions. Show a little empathy. You might discover worries or fears driving their behavior that you hadn’t even considered.
At the end of the day, emotions aren’t roadblocks—they’re signals. When both sides feel seen and heard, even the toughest topics can be tackled with more calm and clarity. So, the real goal isn’t to get rid of feelings during a conversation, but to bring them out into the open, where you can both deal with them honestly and constructively.
